Ironically, Hippolytus used the calculation to cool imminent expectation: he tells of a Syrian bishop who led his flock into the wilderness to meet Christ, and a bishop in Pontus who told his people the end would come within a year, with harmful results. The end was pushed three centuries away. When AD 500 approached, later chronologers simply recalculated.
Even a sober scheme designed to calm speculation becomes a date in its own right; a chronology that pushes the end away can later be used to pull it close.
Pope Gregory I (the Great)

In homilies, the Dialogues and letters Gregory repeatedly taught that the end of the world was near. In his letter of 601 to King Æthelberht of Kent, preserved by Bede, he wrote that the end of the present world was already at hand and the kingdom of the saints was coming.
Plague, famine, floods at Rome, the Lombard invasions of Italy and the collapse of order, read in the light of Luke 21:10–11, 25–26.
The world continued; Gregory's sense of the end shaped his urgency for mission (including the mission to England) and pastoral reform rather than a fixed date. He set no date.
A strong sense of nearness can energise faithful mission without date-setting; Gregory read his catastrophes as signs, but used them to call people to repentance rather than to calculation.
Various preachers and monastic writers in the Latin West
The thousand years of Revelation 20 would end around the millennium of Christ's birth (1000) or of his passion (1033), loosing Satan and bringing Antichrist and the judgment.

A literal counting of Revelation 20:2–7 from the incarnation, signs such as comets and famines, and the tradition about Antichrist summarised in Adso of Montier-en-Der's letter (c. 950). Abbo of Fleury recalled hearing a Paris preacher (c. 975) announce Antichrist for 1000 and opposing him; Raoul Glaber described portents and famines around 1033.

Nothing ended. How widespread the 'terrors of the year 1000' were is disputed: nineteenth-century romantic historians painted mass panic; many twentieth-century historians (and later Sylvain Gouguenheim) dismissed it as a myth because official sources say little; Richard Landes and others argue that apocalyptic expectation was real and significant but under-reported by clerical writers who followed Augustine's ban on dating the end.
Round numbers and anniversaries attract expectation; and the historian's question of how many people believed it is itself contested and should be stated carefully.
c. 1190s (1260 expected)
Joachim of Fiore and his followers

History unfolds in three states, of the Father, the Son and the Spirit; the age of the Son would last forty-two generations of thirty years, so that a new age of the Spirit, preceded by Antichrist, would dawn around 1260.
The 1,260 days of Revelation 11:3 and 12:6 read as years, the forty-two generations of Matthew 1, and an elaborate concordance between the two Testaments.

Joachim himself was cautious about the exact year, but his followers fixed 1260. In 1254 the Franciscan Gerard of Borgo San Donnino proclaimed Joachim's writings as an 'eternal gospel' replacing the New Testament, which was condemned in 1255. The year 1260 saw the great flagellant processions in Italy, but no new age came.
A historical scheme that is suggestive in its author's hands can harden into a date in his disciples' hands.
Pope Gregory IX and papal partisans; Joachite writers
Emperor Frederick II was the beast from the sea and a forerunner or embodiment of Antichrist. Some of Frederick's supporters, in turn, cast him as a divinely sent chastiser of a corrupt church.

Revelation 13 applied to the emperor's conflict with the papacy (Gregory IX's 1239 letter opening 'a beast has risen from the sea'), and pseudo-Joachite prophecies expecting a terrible emperor before 1260.
Frederick died in 1250, ten years before the expected climax. Some refused to believe he was dead and expected his return; legends of a sleeping emperor who would come back persisted for centuries.
Identifying a political opponent as Antichrist is an ancient temptation; the identification usually tells us more about the conflict than about the text.
The Spiritual Franciscans (Peter John Olivi, Ubertino da Casale, Angelo Clareno)
The Franciscan order's commitment to absolute poverty marked the dawn of the final age; corrupt popes such as Boniface VIII were a 'mystical Antichrist' preceding the final Antichrist.
Joachite periodisation, Olivi's Commentary on the Apocalypse (Lectura super Apocalipsim), and the persecution of the poor brothers read as the trials of the last days.

Pope John XXII suppressed the Spirituals; four were burned at Marseille in 1318, and Olivi's commentary was condemned in 1326. The expected renewal did not come, though the movement fed later reform and dissent.
Sincere zeal for holiness, combined with reading one's own persecutors into Revelation, can make the scheme feel self-confirming.
1347–1351 and after
Flagellants and many preachers; later John of Rupescissa

The plague, which killed perhaps a third or more of Europe's population, was the pestilence of the last days and God's final warning; Antichrist was coming soon (Rupescissa expected him in the 1360s).
Luke 21:11 and Revelation 6:8, and the sheer scale of death.

Flagellant bands processed through Europe until Pope Clement VI condemned them in 1349; in several places plague fear and end-time agitation fed murderous attacks on Jews, falsely blamed for the plague. The world went on, and the plague returned periodically for centuries.
A real catastrophe can be read as the last catastrophe; and end-time panic can turn into violence against scapegoats, a moral danger as serious as the exegetical one.
The Taborites, radical Hussites in Bohemia
Christ would come in judgment in February 1420; all towns would be destroyed except five cities of refuge; the faithful should gather on mountains and take up the sword against the wicked.
Matthew 24:16 ('flee to the mountains'), the punishment of Babylon in Revelation 18, and the persecution following the execution of Jan Hus in 1415.

Christ did not come. The Taborites founded the town of Tábor, fought effectively in the Hussite Wars, and some radicals turned to communal and antinomian experiments. The radical armies were destroyed at Lipany in 1434, and Tábor submitted in 1452.
When a predicted end fails, the movement may try to bring it about by force.
Girolamo Savonarola, Dominican preacher in Florence

The sword of the Lord was about to fall on a corrupt Italy and church; the French invasion of 1494 by Charles VIII was its fulfilment, and a repentant Florence would become a new Jerusalem leading the renewal of the church.
Prophetic visions he claimed to have received, Old Testament prophetic patterns of chastisement and renewal, and the Apocalypse.

Florence briefly adopted his moral reforms (including the 'bonfire of the vanities'), but he was excommunicated in 1497 and hanged and burned in 1498. He was a prophet of chastisement and renewal more than a date-setter of the end of the world, and he remains admired by some Catholics and Protestants for his call to reform.
Interpreting a current military event as the fulfilment of one's own prophecy gives a preacher great authority until events turn.
1501–1502 (end expected c. 1656)
Christopher Columbus

The world would last 7,000 years and about 155 years remained; before the end the gospel must reach all nations and Jerusalem be recovered for Christendom, tasks in which he saw his voyages as providential.

Augustine's world-week scheme as calculated by Pierre d'Ailly, Matthew 24:14, Isaiah's prophecies of the islands and the ends of the earth, and medieval prophecy collections, gathered in his Libro de las profecías.
The world did not end around 1656. Historians now recognise that apocalyptic motives mattered to Columbus alongside wealth and glory.
Prophetic calculations have shaped even world-changing secular events, and they are as fallible in great men as in obscure ones.
Martin Luther and many early Protestants
The papacy was the Antichrist of 2 Thessalonians 2 and the Turk was the little horn of Daniel 7 or Gog; the last day was near, and Luther hoped it would not be long delayed.

2 Thessalonians 2:3–4 (the man of lawlessness seated in the temple of God) applied to the papal claims; Daniel 7 and Ezekiel 38–39 applied to the Ottoman advance, which reached the walls of Vienna in 1529; and a world chronology (his Supputatio annorum mundi, 1541) in which the six thousand years would be shortened.

Luther died in 1546 and the world continued. The papal identification became standard in historic Protestant confessions (for example, the Westminster Confession 25.6 as originally written) and is still held by some historicists, while many Protestants today regard it as an overreach or modify it. The Ottoman Empire endured until 1922.
Identifications forged in fierce conflict persuade those inside the conflict; whether they are right is a separate question from whether they produced a correct date, which they did not.
Thomas Müntzer
The fifth kingdom of Daniel 2 was about to break in; the elect must take up the sword to clear away the ungodly and prepare for the reign of God.
Daniel 2 (his 'Sermon to the Princes', 1524), the harvest imagery of Matthew 13, and his belief in direct revelation by the Spirit.
Müntzer joined the Peasants' War; the peasant army was crushed at Frankenhausen on 15 May 1525, and he was executed later that month. Luther strongly opposed him.
When a predicted divine intervention is linked to a political cause, failure costs lives, not only reputations.
Melchior Hoffman, Anabaptist lay preacher
Christ would return in 1533; Strasbourg would be the spiritual Jerusalem from which 144,000 heralds would go out; Hoffman himself was Elijah, one of the two witnesses.
Revelation 7 and 11, a reckoning of time from the apostolic age, and the prophecies of a Strasbourg couple whose visions he trusted.

Hoffman returned to Strasbourg to await the end, was imprisoned there in 1533, and died in prison about ten years later still expecting it. His followers carried his ideas into the Netherlands and then Münster.
A personal role in the prophecy (being Elijah or a witness) makes revision very hard and transfers the scheme to more radical heirs.
Jan Matthys and Jan van Leiden at Münster
Münster was the New Jerusalem; the end would come at Easter 1534; the saints must purge the city and prepare for Christ's kingdom.
Hoffman's scheme transferred from Strasbourg to Münster, the New Jerusalem of Revelation 21, and Old Testament patterns of holy war and kingship.

Matthys rode out against the besiegers at Easter 1534 expecting divine protection and was killed. Jan van Leiden declared himself king, introduced community of goods and polygamy, and ruled under siege until the city fell in June 1535. The leaders were executed in January 1536, and their cages still hang from the tower of St Lambert's Church. Peaceful Anabaptists, such as the Mennonites, later distanced themselves sharply from Münster.
Münster became the cautionary tale that shaped Protestant suspicion of chiliasm for centuries, and it illustrates how disappointment can escalate rather than end a movement.
1593 (end expected 1688–1700)
John Napier of Merchiston
The day of God's judgment would fall between 1688 and 1700.
A historicist reading of Revelation in which the trumpets and vials were mapped onto church history, the papacy was Antichrist, and the prophetic periods were calculated as years.
The judgment did not come. Napier is remembered today chiefly for inventing logarithms (1614); his commentary was nonetheless widely read and translated.
Intelligence and mathematical skill are no protection; the problem lies in the method, not the arithmetic.
1649–1661 (1666 widely expected)
The Fifth Monarchy Men in England
After the four empires of Daniel 2 and 7, the fifth monarchy of Christ and his saints was imminent; the execution of Charles I opened the way, and 1666 (1,000 plus 666) was widely seen as a key year.
Daniel 2:44 and 7:27, the number 666 of Revelation 13:18, and the upheavals of the civil wars.

They first supported and then turned against Cromwell. Thomas Venner led two small armed risings, the second in January 1661, and was executed. In 1666 London suffered plague and the Great Fire, which some saw as signs, but no kingdom came, and the movement dissolved.
Political revolution can feel like the hinge of history to those inside it; when fused with a number game like 1000 + 666, it produces precise disappointment.
Cotton Mather, Boston Puritan minister
Mather expected the end of the present age and Christ's coming in 1697; when that passed he looked to 1716, then 1736.
Historicist calculations from Daniel and Revelation, and events such as wars and earthquakes.

Each date passed (Mather himself died in 1728). The revised dates are often cited; the exact form of each expectation is summarised from secondary literature and may be simplified in popular retellings.
Revising the date after a failure is the commonest response, and it seldom causes a believer to question the method itself.
British and American historicists (e.g. James Bicheno, Edward King, George Stanley Faber)

The French Revolution was the earthquake of Revelation 11:13; the capture of Pope Pius VI by French troops in 1798 ended the 1,260 years of papal supremacy (538–1798) and inflicted the 'deadly wound' of Revelation 13:3; some identified Napoleon as Antichrist or the wilful king of Daniel 11.
The day-year principle applied to the 1,260 days of Daniel 7:25 and Revelation 12–13, and the startling collapse of the old order in Catholic France.

The papacy recovered in 1800 and Napoleon fell in 1815 without the end arriving. The 1798 date was nonetheless absorbed into later historicism and is still held by Seventh-day Adventists and some others as a fulfilled prophetic marker rather than as a prediction of the end; critics see it as a choice of starting and ending points made to fit.
Events of genuine magnitude invite identification; whether an identification is valid depends on the method, which is contested, but predictions of an immediate end built on it failed.
William Miller and the Millerite movement
Christ would return 'about the year 1843', at first reckoned as between 21 March 1843 and 21 March 1844; then, through Samuel Snow's 'seventh-month message', on 22 October 1844.
The 2,300 'evenings and mornings' of Daniel 8:14 read as years from the decree of 457 BC (Ezra 7), with the cleansing of the sanctuary taken to mean the purification of the earth at Christ's coming.

The Great Disappointment of 22 October 1844 shattered tens of thousands. Miller confessed his error in timing but continued to expect Christ soon until his death in 1849. Some followers formed the Advent Christian Church; others, through Hiram Edson, Joseph Bates and Ellen and James White, reinterpreted the event as Christ entering the heavenly sanctuary, which became Seventh-day Adventist doctrine.
Disappointment often leads not to abandoning the date but to spiritualising it: the event is said to have happened invisibly or in heaven.
Charles Taze Russell, the Watch Tower Society and Jehovah's Witnesses

Christ's invisible presence began in 1874 (a date taken from Nelson Barbour); the 'times of the Gentiles' would end in October 1914 with the end of the present order; under J. F. Rutherford, 1925 would see the return of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; in the 1960s and 70s the organisation suggested that 1975, as the end of six thousand years of human history, could bring the millennium.

Seven 'times' (Daniel 4) read as 2,520 years from 607 BC, the Jubilee cycles, and biblical chronology from Adam. Russell's group is not dispensationalist and stands outside historic Trinitarian Christianity, but its dates show the same method at work.

1914 brought the First World War, which was taken as partial vindication; the date was reinterpreted as Christ's invisible enthronement in heaven, and the presence date moved from 1874 to 1914. 1925 passed (a house built in San Diego for the returning patriarchs, Beth Sarim, was sold in 1948). After 1975 the organisation acknowledged that some statements had raised expectations, and many left. The teaching that the generation of 1914 would see the end was revised in 1995 and later.
When a date coincides with a dramatic event, it can be preserved by reinterpreting what was supposed to happen, which makes the system almost impossible to falsify.
Herbert W. Armstrong, Radio Church of God / Worldwide Church of God

Armstrong's publications and ministers pointed to the start of the tribulation or Christ's return at several dates, most famously that the church would flee to Petra in 1972, with Christ returning about three and a half years later, around 1975.

British-Israelism (the belief that the British and American peoples are the lost tribes of Israel), the nineteen-year 'time cycles' of his ministry, and Revelation 12:14 (the woman fleeing to the wilderness).

None of the dates was fulfilled. The 1975 booklet itself did not state an explicit date for Christ's return, and evidence for the earliest dates (1936, sometimes given as 1935, and 1943) comes from later summaries of Plain Truth articles. After Armstrong's death in 1986, his successors under Joseph Tkach renounced his distinctive doctrines and led the church into evangelical orthodoxy, renaming it Grace Communion International in 2009, a rare case of a whole denomination repudiating its prophetic system.
Failed prediction can, over time, lead to genuine reformation as well as to schism.
1970 (implying c. 1988)
Hal Lindsey, The Late Great Planet Earth

The generation that saw Israel reborn in 1948 would see Christ's return; since a biblical generation is about forty years, 'within forty years or so of 1948' all these things could take place, which implied a rapture around 1981 (seven years before) and a return around 1988.
The parable of the fig tree (Matthew 24:32–34) with the fig tree read as Israel, Ezekiel 37–39, and current events: the Soviet Union as Gog, the European Common Market as the revived Roman Empire.

The book became the best-selling non-fiction book of the 1970s. Lindsey hedged ('if this is a correct deduction', 'or so') and never set a fixed day; his later books, such as The 1980s: Countdown to Armageddon (1980), continued to stress the nearness of the end, and after 1988 the forty-year count was quietly dropped by most who had used it. Chuck Smith of Calvary Chapel had written in Future Survival (1978) that he was convinced the Lord would come for his church before the end of 1981, while allowing that he could be wrong.
A hedged implication still functions as a date in readers' minds, and its passing damaged the credibility of prophecy teaching generally.
11–13 September 1988
Edgar C. Whisenant
The rapture would occur at Rosh Hashanah, 11–13 September 1988. Whisenant reportedly said that only if the Bible were in error was he wrong.
The 1948 + 40 generation count, the Feast of Trumpets as the rapture feast, and a long list of calculations ('88 reasons').

Millions of copies of the booklet circulated, and some Christian broadcasters altered their programming. When nothing happened Whisenant moved the date to 1989 and later to other years; each passed. Mainstream dispensational teachers had widely criticised the book beforehand.
Even a strongly anti-date-setting scholarly tradition cannot prevent popular date-setting built on its framework; the guard-rails must be taught as clearly as the framework.
John F. Walvoord; Charles H. Dyer (The Rise of Babylon, 1991); many prophecy broadcasters

Iraq's invasion of Kuwait and the coalition response were setting the stage for Armageddon; Saddam Hussein's reconstruction of ancient Babylon showed that the literal city of Revelation 17–18 would rise again as an economic and religious centre.

Revelation 17–18, Jeremiah 50–51 and Isaiah 13 (read as not yet fully fulfilled because Babylon was never suddenly destroyed), and Saddam's well-publicised rebuilding of Nebuchadnezzar's palace with bricks bearing his own name.

The revised edition of Walvoord's Armageddon, Oil and the Middle East Crisis sold very widely during the crisis. The war ended quickly in 1991; Saddam was overthrown in 2003 and executed in 2006. The rebuilt city never became a world centre, and Babylon was listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage site in 2019. Dyer and others maintain that the prophecy of a future Babylon stands, while acknowledging that Saddam's project was not its fulfilment.
A thesis may survive the failure of a particular identification, but the identification should never have been presented with the confidence it was.
Harold Camping, Family Radio
The end of the world would very probably come in September 1994.
A detailed biblical chronology from creation, Jubilee cycles and symbolic numbers.

Camping titled his book '1994?' and allowed for a small chance of error; when the date passed he said he had miscalculated. He later developed a teaching that the church age had ended and that Christians should leave their churches.
A question mark does not prevent a date from being heard as a prophecy.
Various Christian writers and broadcasters, of different millennial views
The 'millennium bug' in computer date systems might trigger economic and social collapse on 1 January 2000, possibly opening the way for a world government or the end-time scenario.

Real technical concern about two-digit year fields, combined with Revelation 13 and the symbolism of the year 2000. Interestingly, some of the loudest Christian warnings came from the postmillennial Christian Reconstructionist Gary North, not from dispensationalists; Jerry Falwell promoted a video on preparing for Y2K.

Very little disruption occurred, partly because of extensive remediation. Some who had stockpiled supplies or moved to rural areas felt foolish; the experience reinforced scepticism about apocalyptic forecasts.
Round-number anxiety is not unique to any one eschatology, and a real but manageable problem can be inflated into an apocalypse.
21 May and 21 October 2011
The rapture and a great earthquake would occur on 21 May 2011, followed by the destruction of the world on 21 October 2011.
Camping's chronology, which placed creation in 11,013 BC and counted 7,000 years from the flood (Genesis 7:4 and 2 Peter 3:8).

Followers spent savings on billboards and quit jobs. After 21 May Camping said a 'spiritual' judgment had occurred and the end would come in October; after October passed, Family Radio issued a statement in 2012 acknowledging that the prediction had been wrong and sinful, and that Matthew 24:36 should have been heeded. Camping died in 2013.
Disappointment followed by spiritualisation followed by repentance: the whole cycle in one year.
21 December 2012
New Age and popular media writers (not a Christian movement)
The end of a b'ak'tun cycle in the Maya Long Count calendar would bring catastrophe or transformation.
Misreadings of the Maya calendar, combined with pseudoscientific claims about planetary collisions and alignments.
Nothing happened; Maya scholars had stressed that the calendar simply rolled into a new cycle. It is noted here because many Christians were asked about it, and some Christian media amplified it.
Apocalyptic expectation is a human tendency, not only a Christian one; the same patterns appear in secular and non-Christian settings.
April 2014–September 2015
Mark Biltz and John Hagee
A tetrad of four total lunar eclipses falling on Passover and Tabernacles in 2014 and 2015 was a heavenly sign that something momentous for Israel and the world was about to happen.
Genesis 1:14 (lights as 'signs'), Joel 2:31 and Acts 2:20 (the moon turned to blood), and earlier tetrads said to coincide with 1492, 1948–49 and 1967–68.

Both writers said they were not setting a date for Christ's return, but they predicted significant change. No event of the predicted magnitude occurred. Critics, including dispensational scholars, noted that tetrads have occurred many times since the first century without matching events; that the 1492 link was weak (the eclipses were in 1493–94, after the expulsion); that some of the eclipses were not visible from Jerusalem; and that Joel ties the moon's turning to blood to the day of the Lord itself, which Peter applies to Pentecost (Acts 2:16–21).
Signs drawn from the regular movements of the heavens are predictable centuries ahead and so cannot carry the weight placed on them.
23 September 2017
Online prophecy teachers; numerologist David Meade

On 23 September 2017 the constellation Virgo, with the sun at her shoulder, the moon at her feet, Jupiter leaving her 'womb' and nine stars plus three planets over her head, fulfilled the 'great sign' of Revelation 12:1–2; some expected the rapture or the start of the tribulation.
Revelation 12 read as an astronomical event, and the long transit of Jupiter through Virgo.

Nothing happened. Meade's claims (linked to the supposed planet 'Nibiru') were widely reported, but he was not a mainstream Christian teacher, and he later said he had not predicted the end of the world on that day. Astronomers noted that similar arrangements recur; evangelical and dispensational teachers widely criticised the claim beforehand, pointing out that Revelation 12 describes the birth of Christ (12:5) and is seen 'in heaven' in a vision, not in the night sky.
Internet virality rewards novelty, so modern date claims can spread faster and further than the critics who answer them.
Social-media preachers and some popular prophecy commentators
The COVID-19 pandemic was a sign of the end, and vaccines, vaccine passports or digital health certificates were the mark of the beast or its precursor.
Revelation 13:16–17 (no one may buy or sell without the mark), Luke 21:11 (pestilences), and rumours about microchips in vaccines.

The vaccine passport schemes were largely withdrawn by 2022. Many prominent evangelical leaders, including dispensational prophecy teachers, publicly rejected the identification, arguing that the mark of the beast is a deliberate act of worship and allegiance to the beast (Revelation 13:15–16; 14:9–11), not something a believer could take unknowingly through a medical treatment.
Fear of unknowingly taking the mark can do pastoral harm; the text itself presents the mark as a conscious act of loyalty.
Israel's rebirth (1948) and the fig tree
1948 to the present
The founding of the State of Israel on 14 May 1948 fulfils prophecies of Israel's regathering and is the 'budding of the fig tree' that signals the final generation.

Most dispensational writers since 1948, including John Walvoord, J. Dwight Pentecost, Hal Lindsey, Arnold Fruchtenbaum and Thomas Ice; also many historic premillennialists, and some Reformed and postmillennial writers who expect a future mass conversion of Jews (Romans 11).

Scripture repeatedly promises that God will gather Israel 'from all the nations' to its own land in the last days (Isaiah 11:11–12; Jeremiah 30–31; Ezekiel 36:24; 37:1–14; Amos 9:14–15). For nearly two thousand years this seemed impossible, and many Christians spiritualised it. Yet a dispersed people returned, revived a dead language and formed a state, an event without historical parallel. Ezekiel 37 even describes a two-stage restoration, bones coming together before the breath of life, which fits a return in unbelief before national repentance. If God's promises to Israel stand (Romans 11:28–29), the return cannot be dismissed as coincidence, and Jesus told us to 'learn the lesson of the fig tree' (Matthew 24:32).

Exegetically, many prophecies of return were fulfilled in the return from Babylon (Ezra 1; Jeremiah 29:10), and the New Testament locates the fulfilment of Israel's hopes in Christ and in a renewed people of Jews and Gentiles (Acts 15:15–17; Galatians 3:29; Ephesians 2:11–22), so amillennial and many covenant critics deny that a modern secular state is the subject of those prophecies. Several promises (Deuteronomy 30:1–5; Ezekiel 36:24–28) put repentance at or before the return, whereas 1948 was largely secular. The fig-tree identification is weak: Luke's version says 'the fig tree and all the trees' (Luke 21:29), showing an illustration from nature, not a symbol of Israel. Preterist critics add that the 'lesson of the fig tree' concerns the signs before AD 70. Historically, the identification produced the 1948 + 40 = 1988 counting that failed, and earlier premillennialists (before 1948) had expected the return to come only after the rapture, so the system adjusted to events.

Dispensational scholars answer that the return-in-unbelief stage is precisely what Ezekiel 37 and 36 (gathering before cleansing) and Zechariah 12:10 anticipate; that the return from Babylon did not exhaust passages promising a gathering 'a second time' (Isaiah 11:11) from 'all nations'; and that Romans 11:25–29 envisages a future for ethnic Israel. Many, including Thomas Ice and Arnold Fruchtenbaum, separate the significance of 1948 from the fig-tree argument and reject counting from 1948; Ice reads 'this generation' as the generation that will see the tribulation signs, not those alive in 1948. They prefer to call 1948 'stage-setting': it makes the end-time scenario possible but fulfils nothing on a timetable, and the rapture remains imminent and signless.

That a scattered people re-established a nation in its ancestral land is a remarkable historical fact that Christians of several millennial views find theologically significant, especially in the light of Romans 11. Whether it is the fulfilment of specific Old Testament prophecies depends on prior decisions about how the New Testament applies Israel's promises, which divide the views fundamentally. The fig-tree inference, and especially generation-counting from 1948, is weak and is rejected by many dispensational scholars themselves; the strongest premillennial position treats 1948 as possible stage-setting, not as a clock.
